# Testing a Coefficient

## Testing a Coefficient Against a Benchmark Value

**The goal of this section:** ask whether an estimate is distinguishable from
zero, and be exact about what that question is.

An estimate of 1.52 euro a year is large or small only against something. The
only thing we have to compare it with is its own sampling variation.

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
t = \frac{\hat{\beta}_1 - 0}{\mathrm{se}(\hat{\beta}_1)}
\end{equation}
```

- $\hat{\beta}_1$: our estimate, from our one sample
- $\mathrm{se}(\hat{\beta}_1)$: the estimated spread of last week's histogram
- $0$: the value we are testing against, which is a choice

::: {.caveat title="Zero is a choice, not a default"}
Nothing makes zero special except that it is often the interesting comparison.
If theory says the return should be two euro, test against two.
:::

<!-- IDEA 1. 10-35 min. -->

## What Rejecting Does and Does Not Mean

::: {.defn title="What a rejection says"}
If the true return were zero, a sample like ours would be unusual.
:::

::: {.caveat title="What it does not say"}
It does not say the true return is 1.52. It does not say the return is large.
It does not say the finding matters. And it says nothing at all about whether
schooling causes earnings.
:::

## Vote: Would You Reject at Five Per Cent?

An estimate of 0.40 with a standard error of 0.19.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what is the largest
standard error that would still let you reject?
:::

<!-- ConcepTest 1. The arithmetic is easy; the second question is the one
     that shows whether they understand what the ratio is doing. -->

# Confidence Intervals for an Effect

## Reporting an Interval Instead of a Point Estimate

**The goal of this section:** report the estimate and its precision in one
object, instead of throwing the precision away.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-4_interval.png}{The sampling distribution implied by
our estimate and its standard error. The shaded region is the 95 per cent
interval; the dashed line is the null.}
```

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. -->

## Reading the Interval Out Loud

::: {.worked title="The sentence"}
Our estimate of the return to a year of schooling is 1.52 euro an hour, with a
95 per cent confidence interval from [lower] to [upper].
:::

::: {.caveat title="What the 95 per cent counts"}
It counts intervals, not truths. If we repeated the whole exercise many times,
about 95 per cent of the intervals we built this way would contain the true
return. This particular interval either contains it or does not.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
The test is inside the picture: the interval excludes zero exactly when the
test rejects at five per cent. They are the same statement, and the interval
is the more informative way to say it.
:::

## Vote: Which Interval Is More Useful?

An estimate of 1.5 with an interval from $-0.1$ to $3.1$, or an estimate of
0.4 with an interval from 0.3 to 0.5.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: which one would you act on, and does that match
which one is significant?
:::

<!-- ConcepTest 2. The second is significant and small; the first is not
     significant and might be large. Most rooms pick on the star. Do not
     adjudicate. -->

# Reading a Regression Table

## The Same Estimate at Four Different Sample Sizes

**The goal of this section:** read published output the way a referee reads
it, starting with the right number.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-4_studies.png}{Four studies reporting an identical
return to schooling. Only the sample size differs.}
```

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. -->

## Why Significance Is About Precision, Not Effect Size

Every one of those four found the same effect. Two of them would be published
as a finding and two as a null result.

::: {.result}
Significance is a statement about how precisely you measured something. It is
not a statement about how big the something is, and the two get confused in
print constantly.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
This is also why a large study can report a significant effect that nobody
should act on, and a small one can miss an effect that matters.
:::

## What to Read First in a Regression Table

1. **The coefficient, in units.** What does it mean in euro?
2. **The standard error.** How precisely was it measured?
3. **The sample size and what it is a sample of.**
4. **What else is in the regression**, which is week 8.
5. **The stars**, last, if at all.

::: {.caveat}
A table with stars and no standard errors is hiding the number you most need.
When you build your own, report the interval.
:::

## Vote: What Is Missing From This Table?

[Show a published table with stars, no standard errors, and no sample size.]

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: could you tell from it whether the effect is
large?
:::

<!-- ConcepTest 3. No, and that is the point. Do not adjudicate. -->

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: significance is not size, and size is not
importance. A star tells you about the standard error. It tells you nothing
about whether the number matters.]

<!-- 92-97 min. Same slot every week. They answer in pairs first, then
     you. Not that causation is hard in the abstract, but that THIS
     estimate rests on something nameable that may well be false. -->

## Application

Take the same estimate and report it four ways: bare, with a standard error,
with an interval, and with a star.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote first: which of the four would you want if you were deciding whether to
stay in education another year? Take the vote before we discuss.
:::

Lab this week: building a regression table in R, and reading someone else's.

<!-- 97-105 min. ConcepTest 4. -->

## Three Ways to Report One Number

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Testing a Coefficient.** A t-statistic compares an estimate to its own standard error, and to nothing else.
2. **Confidence Intervals for an Effect.** An interval carries the estimate and its precision in one object.
3. **Reading a Regression Table.** A table is a set of claims, each with a standard error attached - read those first.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Next week: what happens when a second variable enters, and what holding it fixed actually buys you.
:::

## Derivation: Where the t-Statistic Comes From

Standardise the estimator by its own estimated standard error and show what
distribution the result has.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Start from the sampling distribution of the slope, divide by the
standard error, and account for the fact that the standard error is itself
estimated. The step that does the work is the third: it is the only reason the
answer is a t and not a normal, and it is why the difference stops mattering
once the sample is large.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]
